newsitem.title: USA: NYMEX oil ends down, fundamentals winning struggle.
newsitem.headline: NYMEX oil ends down, fundamentals winning struggle.

text.p: NYMEX crude oil futures prices ended mostly lower, while refined products settled lower across the board, as the market's fundamentals began to gain the upper hand on recent speculative, technical dealings.
Crude oil for July delivery on the New York Mercantile Exchange lost 21 cents to end at $20.12 a barrel after trading between $20.38 and $20.08.
July unleaded gasoline fell 1.02 cents, closing at 60.42 cents a gallon. July heating oil settled at 54.16 cents a gallon, down 0.46 cent.

Extending Tuesday's declines, Wednesday's losses were believed to be confirmation that the market's current fundamentals are more powerful than the speculative dealings that have confounded traders in recent weeks.

Despite consistently ample crude supply, steady foreign imports and weakening cash-market differentials, commodity funds in the past month have coerced the market into areas that many traders said it never belonged.

Inventory data from the American Petroleum Institute (API) released Tuesday, and from the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) on Wednesday, showed rising inventories in crude, distillates and unleaded gasoline, even though refinery capacity utilization maintained a torrid production pace in the past week.
In political arenas, threats of supply disruptions have failed to materialize.

The United Nations Security Council formally approved the renewal of the Iraqi oil-for-food accord on Wednesday, as expected. Over the past week, Tehran and Washington have made somewhat friendlier comments toward one another following the election of a political moderate to Iran's presidency.
Most traders and analysts expect little change in the market when OPEC member nations meet June 25.

On top of it all, peak-season demand for unleaded gasoline - needed to help underpin crude sentiment at this time of year - has been tepid at best. With refinery production as robust as it has been, running at an unheard-of 100.4-percent rate in the last week, according to the DOE, traders fear gasoline supplies will weigh on the complex.

"Overall, the market seems to have discounted most of the bad news, like the APIs and the Iraqi renewal. We'll probably need fresh bearish news to push below $20 (a barrel, basis July), and we're probably going to get it," said Jim Ritterbusch at Sweeney Oil.
"It may come in the form of the Commitment of Traders report this Friday, which I expect will indicate speculators are still net long in this market," Ritterbusch said.
Ritterbusch said it was only a matter of time before the fundamentals in the market would begin to lead valuations.
"They are decidedly bearish, in my opinion. In the short term, funds may push (prices) around, but over time the fundamentals rear their ugly head, and I think that's what's happening here," he said.
"At some point we've got to look at this evolving situation and say, 'Wow, crude stocks are building in midst of the highest refinery usage we've seen in two years.'"
Ritterbusch said refined products futures were likely to lead the complex in the near term as the market tries to get a better feel for whether summer gasoline demand will kick in soon.
He has a price target of $19.25 a barrel by the end of next week.
